title: I'm eating
goal: Say what's going on right now with *ag* + verbal noun — the structure used most in everyday conversation.
bekal: build *Tá mé ag …* for actions in progress
recognize verbal nouns and use them with an object
ask *Cad atá tú a dhéanamh?* and answer it

notes: **Ag + verbal noun = "-ing".** Irish doesn't change the verb to say something is in progress; it uses *tá* plus the preposition *ag* plus a special form called the **verbal noun**. *Tá mé ag ithe* is literally "I am at eating" — exactly the old English form that survives in *a-hunting we will go*.

**The verbal noun really is a noun.** So its object goes into the possessive (genitive) form: *leabhar* becomes *ag léamh leabhair*, *peil* becomes *ag imirt peile* — literally "at the reading of a book", "at the playing of football". At A1 you don't need to build the genitive yourself — just learn the common pairs, and if in doubt, leave the noun as it is. Native speakers will still understand you.

**Ag féachaint ar, ag éisteacht le — some bring their own preposition.** *Féach* is always followed by *ar* ("look **at**"), *éist* by *le* ("listen **to**"), *fan* by *le* for "wait **for**". The preposition belongs to the verb and has to be learned with it, just like English "listen **to**".

**Cad atá tú a dhéanamh? — a question to learn whole.** Its structure breaks the usual pattern because there's a clause inside it, which is only fully explained at A2. For now learn three forms: *Cad atá tú a dhéanamh?* (what are you doing?), *Cad atá sé a dhéanamh?* (what's he doing?), and the answer *Tá mé ag …*

sections.title: Thirty of the most common verbal nouns

blocks.text: The first column is the ready-to-use form — just put it after *Tá mé*. The last column is the base form, which you'll need to look the verb up in a dictionary and for Unit 10.

blocks.title: How the ag form is made from the base
items: There's no single rule. Some add *-adh* (*glan* → *glanadh*), some *-áil* (*fág* → *fágáil*), some *-acht* (*fan* → *fanacht*), and some change completely (*téigh* → *dul*, *tar* → *teacht*, *déan* → *déanamh*).
That's why this form is **always listed in the dictionary** right after the base, and the best approach is to learn the two together as a pair.
The full list of sixty verbs with their *ag* forms is in the chapter "The sixty most common verbs" at the back of this book.

*Ag caint* ("talking") is an exception worth knowing: it's built from the **noun** *caint*, and has no verb of its own. For the habitual form you use *labhair* → *labhraím*. So *Tá mé ag caint léi* is right, but the verb is *Labhraím léi*.

sections.title: Doing now, doing then, doing later

blocks.text: Only the verb *bí* in front changes; the *ag …* part isn't touched at all. That's why this structure is so useful: once you know the *ag* form, you can use it in all three tenses without learning anything else.
*Bhí* ("was") and *beidh* ("will be") are covered fully in Units 17 and 18. For now, just recognize them when you hear them.

blocks.title: Ag ól tae — but ag ól an tae?
items: If the object is **general** (no *an*), just put it after: *ag ól tae*, *ag ithe aráin*, *ag ceannach bainne*.

If the object is **specific** (with *an*), Irish builds it differently — and that's A2 material. For now, if you need a specific object, use an ordinary present-tense sentence (Unit 10) instead of the *ag* structure.
The good news: nine out of ten everyday sentences use general objects, so the *ag* structure covers almost everything you need.
I — eat
she — drink coffee
they — work
we — learn Irish
you — read
he — sleep
